newsitem.title: USA: Mars probe blasts off for the Red Planet.
newsitem.headline: Mars probe blasts off for the Red Planet.

text.p: A U.S. Mars probe blasted off from Florida on Thursday, beginning a 10-month, interplanetary voyage to the Red Planet.
The Mars Global Surveyor soared aloft at 12:00 p.m. EST (1700 GMT) atop a McDonnell Douglas Corp. Delta 2 rocket launched from Cape Canaveral Air Station.
Bad weather had delayed Surveyor's launch for one day, but everything went smoothly under clear skies on Thursday.

"We have liftoff of NASA's Mars Global Surveyor as America begins its journey back to the Red Planet," said NASA launch commentator Bruce Buckingham as the slim probe headed toward space in a burst of fire.
From an altitude of 230 miles (370 km), the probe's telephoto camera will see objects on Mars' surface as small as a compact car.
By the end of one Martian year -- 687 Earth days -- 99 percent of the planet will have been mapped by Surveyor's electronic eye.
Surveyor is the first of three spacecraft, two U.S. and one Russian, destined for the Red Planet this year. NASA plans to send pairs of spacecraft to the planet every 26 months through to 2005.
NASA had until Nov. 25 to get the probe off the launch pad, or face a 26-month wait for Mars and Earth to realign and allow the mission.
The spacecraft was designed and built in record time to replace NASA's $1 billion Mars Observer probe, which was lost in 1993 just days before it was due to enter orbit about the Red Planet.
Surveyor carries identical copies of five of the seven scientific instruments on its ill-fated predecessor, but at $215 million is much cheaper.

The probe is due to slip into an egg-shapped orbit around Mars on Sept. 12, 1997. The probe will lower and circularize its orbit by dipping into the thin Martian atmosphere and using its wing-like solar panels as air brakes.
